statement: Let $X$ be a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) in which every point has a [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) open neighborhood. Then $X$ is metrizable (Smirnov metrization theorem).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [paracompact](c:paracompact-space): every open cover has a locally finite open refinement.
The space $X$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
Every point of $X$ has an open neighborhood that is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space).

conclusion: The topology of $X$ comes from a metric.

proofs.name: Locally finite pieces and Nagata-Smirnov
proofs.slogan: Cover the space by locally finite metrizable pieces, collect their countably locally finite bases into one, and apply the Nagata-Smirnov theorem.
proofs.scope: The Smirnov member of the family of metrization theorems; the Urysohn, Nagata-Smirnov and Bing members have their own records. The proof reduces to the Nagata-Smirnov theorem.

roles.why: [Paracompactness](c:paracompact-space) gives normality and a locally finite cover by metrizable open sets.
The [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) property makes the normal space regular and separates points.
Local [metrizability](c:metrizable-space) supplies the metrizable open sets that cover $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that $X$ is [normal](c:normal-space) and therefore regular.
steps.detail: A paracompact Hausdorff space is normal (Dieudonne). A normal Hausdorff space separates a point from a closed set that misses it, so $X$ is [regular](c:regular-space).

steps.slogan: Cover $X$ by a [locally finite](c:locally-finite-family) family of metrizable open sets.
steps.detail: The metrizable open neighborhoods cover $X$. Paracompactness gives a locally finite open refinement $\{U_\alpha\}$. An open subset of a metrizable set is metrizable, so every $U_\alpha$ is metrizable.

steps.slogan: Shrink the cover to open sets $W_\alpha$ whose closures lie in $U_\alpha$.
steps.detail: A locally finite open cover of a normal space has a closed shrinking $F_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$ that still covers $X$. Normality gives open $W_\alpha$ with $F_\alpha \subseteq W_\alpha \subseteq \overline{W_\alpha} \subseteq U_\alpha$. The family $\{W_\alpha\}$ is locally finite and covers $X$.

steps.slogan: Choose a countably locally finite base inside each metrizable piece $U_\alpha$.
steps.detail: A metrizable space has a base $\mathcal{B}_\alpha = \bigcup_n \mathcal{B}_{\alpha,n}$ with every $\mathcal{B}_{\alpha,n}$ locally finite (the easy half of the Nagata-Smirnov theorem). Let $\mathcal{B}^*_{\alpha,n}$ hold the members of $\mathcal{B}_{\alpha,n}$ that lie inside $W_\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Show that each family $\mathcal{B}_n = \bigcup_\alpha \mathcal{B}^*_{\alpha,n}$ is locally finite in $X$.
steps.detail: A point outside $U_\alpha$ has a neighborhood that misses $W_\alpha$, since $\overline{W_\alpha} \subseteq U_\alpha$. A point inside the open set $U_\alpha$ sees $\mathcal{B}_{\alpha,n}$ locally finite. Local finiteness of $\{W_\alpha\}$ then gives local finiteness of $\mathcal{B}_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the union of the families $\mathcal{B}_n$ is a base of $X$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in O$ with $O$ open. Choose $\alpha$ with $x \in F_\alpha \subseteq W_\alpha$. Then $O \cap W_\alpha$ is open in $U_\alpha$, so some $B \in \mathcal{B}_\alpha$ has $x \in B \subseteq O \cap W_\alpha$, and $B$ lies in some $\mathcal{B}^*_{\alpha,n}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the regular space $X$ with a countably locally finite base is metrizable.
steps.detail: The space $X$ is regular and Hausdorff by step 1, and it has a base that is a countable union of locally finite families by steps 5 and 6. The Nagata-Smirnov theorem gives a metric that induces the topology of $X$.

concepts.c:paracompact-space: It supplies locally finite refinements and, with the Hausdorff property, normality.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: It is needed for normality and for the metrization theorem.
concepts.c:metrizable-space: Metrizable pieces carry the countably locally finite bases that are assembled.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality allows the shrinkings of the cover.
concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity is the separation axiom that the Nagata-Smirnov theorem requires.
concepts.c:locally-finite-family: Local finiteness of the cover controls local finiteness of the assembled base.

source.note: J. R. Munkres, Topology, 2nd edition, Theorem 42.1 (Smirnov metrization theorem); it reduces to the Nagata-Smirnov theorem.

statement: Let $s$ be a [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real vector space and $f \colon s \to \mathbb{R}$ a [concave function](c:concave-function). If $t \subseteq s$ and $x$ lies in the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $t$, then $f(y) \le f(x)$ for some $y \in t$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [concave](c:concave-function) on the [convex set](c:convex-set) $s$.
The set $t$ is a subset of $s$.
The point $x$ lies in the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $t$.

formal.difference: The declaration works over any linearly ordered field of scalars and any linearly ordered module of values; here both are the reals. It is the dual of the maximum principle ConvexOn.exists_ge_of_mem_convexHull.

proofs.name: Jensen on a finite combination
proofs.slogan: Write $x$ as a finite convex combination of points of $t$ and compare the weighted average of their values with $f(x)$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; the hypothesis $x \in \operatorname{conv} t$ forces $t \ne \emptyset$.

roles.why: A point of the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) is a finite convex combination of points of $t$.
The points of $t$ lie in $s$, where $f$ is concave.
[Concavity](c:concave-function) gives Jensen's inequality for the finite combination.

steps.slogan: Write $x$ as a finite convex combination of points of $t$.
steps.detail: A point of the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $t$ has the form $x = \sum_i w_i p_i$ with $p_i \in t$, $w_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i w_i = 1$. Drop the terms with $w_i = 0$, so that every $w_i > 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the weighted average of the values $f(p_i)$ by $f(x)$.
steps.detail: All $p_i$ lie in $t \subseteq s$ and $f$ is [concave](c:concave-function) on $s$. Jensen's inequality gives $\sum_i w_i f(p_i) \le f(\sum_i w_i p_i) = f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Find an index $i$ with $f(p_i)$ at most the weighted average.
steps.detail: Suppose $f(p_i) > f(x)$ for every $i$. Because all $w_i > 0$, then $\sum_i w_i f(p_i) > f(x) \sum_i w_i = f(x)$, which contradicts step 2. So some $i$ has $f(p_i) \le f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Take $y = p_i$ as the required point of $t$.
steps.detail: The point $y = p_i$ lies in $t$ and satisfies $f(y) \le f(x)$, which is the claim.

concepts.c:convex-hull: The hull is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $t$.
concepts.c:concave-function: Concavity gives Jensen's inequality, the only analytic input.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of $s$ keeps every convex combination of points of $t$ inside $s$.

source.note: mathlib dualizes ConvexOn.exists_ge_of_mem_convexHull: it writes x as a centerMass of points of t (convexHull_eq) and applies ConcaveOn.exists_le_of_centerMass, which rests on the Jensen inequality ConcaveOn.le_map_centerMass.

statement: For every dimension $n \ge 2$ there is a lattice $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ whose [lattice packing](c:lattice-packing) of equal balls (a [sphere packing](c:sphere-packing)) has density at least $\zeta(n)/2^{n-1}$, where $\zeta$ is the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function).

hypotheses.text: The dimension satisfies $n \ge 2$, so that $\zeta(n)$ is a convergent series.

conclusion: Some lattice in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has packing density at least $\zeta(n)/2^{n-1}$.

proofs.name: Siegel mean value theorem
proofs.slogan: Average the number of primitive lattice vectors in a ball over all lattices of covolume 1 and find a lattice with none.
proofs.scope: All dimensions $n \ge 2$. The proof is an outline: Siegel's mean value theorem is the cited ingredient, and the rest is written out.

roles.why: For $n \ge 2$ the sum defining $\zeta(n)$ converges, and the mean value formula holds.

steps.slogan: Average over the space of lattices of covolume 1 with its invariant probability measure.
steps.detail: Let $X_n = SL_n(\mathbb{R})/SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ be the space of lattices of covolume 1 in $\mathbb{R}^n$. It has a finite invariant measure, which we normalize to a probability measure $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Compute the mean number of primitive lattice vectors in a set with Siegel's formula.
steps.detail: Siegel's theorem gives $\int_{X_n} \sum_{v \in \Lambda \setminus 0} f(v)\, d\mu = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f$ for bounded Riemann integrable $f$ with bounded support. Möbius inversion over the multiples $kv$ turns it into $\int \sum_{v\ \mathrm{primitive}} f(v)\, d\mu = \zeta(n)^{-1} \int f$, since $\sum_k \mu(k) k^{-n} = 1/\zeta(n)$.

steps.slogan: Take an open ball of volume below $2\zeta(n)$ and bound the expected count below 2.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be the open ball of radius $r$ centered at $0$ with volume $V < 2\zeta(n)$, and let $f$ be its indicator. The mean number of primitive vectors of $\Lambda$ in $B$ is $V/\zeta(n) < 2$.

steps.slogan: Find a lattice with no primitive vector in the ball, hence no nonzero point in it.
steps.detail: Primitive vectors come in pairs $\pm v$, so their number is even. A nonnegative even integer with mean below 2 is $0$ for some lattice $\Lambda_V$. A nonzero lattice vector is $kv$ with $v$ primitive and $k \ge 1$, and $v \in B$ because $B$ is star-shaped, so $\Lambda_V \cap B = \{0\}$.

steps.slogan: Let $V$ tend to $2\zeta(n)$ and pass to a limit lattice.
steps.detail: Balls of radius $r/2$ around the points of $\Lambda_V$ do not overlap, so they pack with density $V/2^n$. The lattices $\Lambda_V$ have no short vectors, so Mahler's compactness theorem gives a limit lattice with no nonzero point in the open ball of volume $2\zeta(n)$. Its density is $2\zeta(n)/2^n = \zeta(n)/2^{n-1}$.

concepts.c:lattice-packing: The packing by balls centered at lattice points is the object whose density is bounded.
concepts.c:sphere-packing: Disjoint balls around lattice points form the packing whose density is estimated.
concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: The constant $\zeta(n)$ comes from counting primitive vectors in the mean value formula.

source.ref: C. L. Siegel, A mean value theorem in geometry of numbers, Annals of Mathematics 46 (1945), 340-347
source.note: Siegel proves the mean value theorem over the space of lattices and derives the Minkowski-Hlawka bound from it; Hlawka first proved the theorem in 1943.

statement: Let $\rho$ be a [density matrix](c:density-matrix) on $H_A \otimes H_B$ with finite-dimensional factors, possibly [entangled](c:entanglement). Whatever measurement Alice makes on $A$, the outcome probabilities of every measurement of Bob on $B$, summed over Alice's outcomes, are the same.

hypotheses.text: The joint state $\rho$ is a [density matrix](c:density-matrix) on $H_A \otimes H_B$, and both factors have finite dimension.
Alice measures on $A$ alone, with operators $M_k \ge 0$ on $H_A$ that satisfy $\sum_k M_k = I_A$.
Bob measures on $B$ alone, with operators $E_b \ge 0$ on $H_B$ that satisfy $\sum_b E_b = I_B$.

conclusion: The marginal probability $\sum_k p(k,b)$ equals $\operatorname{Tr}(E_b \rho_B)$ with $\rho_B = \operatorname{Tr}_A \rho$, so it does not depend on Alice's measurement.

proofs.name: Reduced state
proofs.slogan: Sum the joint probabilities over Alice's outcomes, use $\sum_k M_k = I_A$, and read the result off the reduced state of Bob.
proofs.scope: Finite dimensions and POVM measurements. A local operation with Kraus operators $K_k$ is included through $M_k = K_k^\dagger K_k$, and a product state is a special case.

roles.why: The Born rule for $\rho$ gives the joint probabilities, and $\rho_B$ is its [partial trace](c:partial-trace).
The completeness relation $\sum_k M_k = I_A$ removes Alice's measurement from the marginal.
Bob's operators $E_b$ give the outcomes whose probabilities are compared.

steps.slogan: Write the joint outcome probabilities of the two local measurements.
steps.detail: Alice's outcome $k$ and Bob's outcome $b$ occur together with probability $p(k,b) = \operatorname{Tr}[(M_k \otimes E_b)\rho]$, by the Born rule for the product operator $M_k \otimes E_b$.

steps.slogan: Sum over Alice's outcomes to get Bob's marginal probability.
steps.detail: By linearity of the trace, $\sum_k p(k,b) = \operatorname{Tr}[(\sum_k M_k \otimes E_b)\rho] = \operatorname{Tr}[(I_A \otimes E_b)\rho]$, because $\sum_k M_k = I_A$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the marginal with the [partial trace](c:partial-trace) over $A$.
steps.detail: The reduced state $\rho_B = \operatorname{Tr}_A \rho$ is defined by $\operatorname{Tr}[(I_A \otimes X)\rho] = \operatorname{Tr}[X \rho_B]$ for every operator $X$ on $H_B$. With $X = E_b$ this gives $\sum_k p(k,b) = \operatorname{Tr}[E_b \rho_B]$.

steps.slogan: Compare two choices of Alice and see that Bob's statistics agree.
steps.detail: The value $\operatorname{Tr}[E_b \rho_B]$ contains neither the operators $M_k$ nor the number of outcomes. So two measurements of Alice, or no measurement at all, give Bob the same statistics, even when $\rho$ is [entangled](c:entanglement).

concepts.c:density-matrix: The joint state fixes all outcome probabilities through the Born rule.
concepts.c:partial-trace: The partial trace over $A$ gives the reduced state that Bob's statistics depend on.
concepts.c:entanglement: The argument never uses a product form, so it holds for entangled states.

source.note: Standard argument from the Born rule and the definition of the partial trace; see the reduced density operator in Nielsen and Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, section 2.4.3.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) and $B$ a real number. Only finitely many $x \in K$ have logarithmic [height](c:height) $\log H_K(x) \le B$, where $H_K(x) = \prod_v \max(1, |x|_v)^{n_v}$ runs over the places $v$ of $K$ with local degrees $n_v$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field): a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.
The bound $B$ is a real number.

conclusion: The set $\{x \in K : \log H_K(x) \le B\}$ is finite.

proofs.name: Denominator and conjugate bounds
proofs.slogan: A bounded height bounds a denominator and all conjugates, and only finitely many algebraic integers have bounded conjugates.
proofs.scope: For $B < 0$ the set is empty because $H_K \ge 1$, so let $B \ge 0$ and $M = e^B$. The height here is the relative height of $K$, which is $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ times the absolute height.

roles.why: Finite degree gives finitely many embeddings and the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) that holds the numerators.
The bound $B$ turns into the bounds $n \le M$ and $|\sigma(x)| \le M$.

steps.slogan: Bound a common denominator of $x$ by the height.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak{d} = \{a \in \mathcal{O}_K : ax \in \mathcal{O}_K\}$ be the denominator ideal of $x$. The finite places contribute exactly $N(\mathfrak{d})$ to $H_K(x)$ and the infinite places contribute factors at least 1. So $n = N(\mathfrak{d}) \le H_K(x) \le M$, and $n \in \mathfrak{d}$ makes $nx$ an [algebraic integer](c:algebraic-integer).

steps.slogan: Bound every conjugate of the integer $nx$ by $M^2$.
steps.detail: For an embedding $\sigma \colon K \to \mathbb{C}$, the place of $\sigma$ contributes at least $\max(1, |\sigma(x)|)$ to $H_K(x)$, and all other factors are at least 1. So $|\sigma(x)| \le M$, and $|\sigma(nx)| = n|\sigma(x)| \le M^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that only finitely many algebraic integers of $K$ have all conjugates bounded.
steps.detail: Let $y \in \mathcal{O}_K$ have $|\sigma(y)| \le C$ for all embeddings, and let $d = [K:\mathbb{Q}]$. Then $y$ is a root of $\prod_\sigma (T - \sigma(y))$, which has integer coefficients bounded by $\binom{d}{j} C^j$. There are finitely many such polynomials, each with finitely many roots.

steps.slogan: Combine the finitely many denominators with the finite sets of numerators.
steps.detail: Each $x$ with $\log H_K(x) \le B$ equals $y/n$ with $1 \le n \le M$ and $y \in \mathcal{O}_K$ with all conjugates at most $M^2$. There are finitely many $n$ and, by step 3, finitely many $y$ for each $n$. So the set of such $x$ is finite.

concepts.c:number-field: Its finite degree gives finitely many embeddings and a ring of integers.
concepts.c:height: The height measures the size of $x$ through denominators and conjugates.
concepts.c:ring-of-integers: The integers $y = nx$ lie in the ring of integers of $K$.
concepts.c:algebraic-integer: Algebraic integers with bounded conjugates are finite in number.

source.note: mathlib bounds a denominator by the height (exists_nat_le_mulHeight₁), shows that integers with bounded conjugates are finite (finite_setOfPred_prod_infinitePlace_iSup_le via Embeddings.finite_of_norm_le), and takes the union over the denominators; the log version follows from the multiplicative one.

statement: Let $\rho = \int P(\alpha)\,|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|\,d^2\alpha$ be a state with a [Glauber-Sudarshan P representation](c:glauber-sudarshan-p-representation) over [coherent states](c:coherent-state), and let $O = \sum c_{mn}\, a^{\dagger m} a^n$ be a finite [normally ordered](c:normal-ordering) operator. Then $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho O) = \int P(\alpha)\, O_N(\alpha,\alpha^*)\, d^2\alpha$ with $O_N = \sum c_{mn}\, \alpha^{*m}\alpha^n$.

hypotheses.text: The state $\rho$ of one mode has the P representation $\rho = \int P(\alpha)\,|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|\,d^2\alpha$.
The operator $O$ is a finite sum of [normally ordered](c:normal-ordering) monomials $a^{\dagger m} a^n$.

conclusion: The quantum expectation $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho O)$ equals the phase-space average of $O_N$ with weight $P$.

proofs.name: Coherent-state diagonal
proofs.slogan: Insert the P representation into the trace and evaluate each normally ordered monomial in a coherent state.
proofs.scope: Finite sums of monomials and a $P$ for which the integral exists; a singular $P$ is read as a distribution acting on the polynomial $O_N$. Other orderings (the Husimi $Q$ function for anti-normal order, the Wigner function for symmetric order) are the other members of the family.

roles.why: The [P representation](c:glauber-sudarshan-p-representation) writes $\rho$ as a weighted sum of [coherent-state](c:coherent-state) projectors.
Normal order puts every $a^\dagger$ left of every $a$, so a coherent state gives a polynomial.

steps.slogan: State the eigenvalue equations of the coherent state $|\alpha\rangle$.
steps.detail: A [coherent state](c:coherent-state) is an eigenvector of the annihilation operator: $a|\alpha\rangle = \alpha|\alpha\rangle$. Taking adjoints gives $\langle\alpha|a^\dagger = \alpha^*\langle\alpha|$, and $\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle = 1$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the normally ordered monomial $a^{\dagger m}a^n$ in the state $|\alpha\rangle$.
steps.detail: All creation operators stand left of all annihilation operators. Step 1 gives $\langle\alpha|a^{\dagger m}a^n|\alpha\rangle = \alpha^{*m}\alpha^n\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle = \alpha^{*m}\alpha^n$.

steps.slogan: Insert the P representation into the trace and move the trace inside the integral.
steps.detail: The trace is linear, so it passes under the integral sign and acts on each projector. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho O) = \int P(\alpha)\operatorname{Tr}(|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|O)\,d^2\alpha = \int P(\alpha)\langle\alpha|O|\alpha\rangle\,d^2\alpha$, by cyclicity of the trace.

steps.slogan: Sum over the monomials of $O$ to obtain $O_N(\alpha,\alpha^*)$.
steps.detail: By linearity and step 2, $\langle\alpha|O|\alpha\rangle = \sum c_{mn}\alpha^{*m}\alpha^n = O_N(\alpha,\alpha^*)$. Substituting this into step 3 gives the claim.

concepts.c:glauber-sudarshan-p-representation: It reduces the quantum trace to an average over coherent-state diagonals.
concepts.c:coherent-state: Coherent states are eigenvectors of the annihilation operator.
concepts.c:normal-ordering: Normal order makes the coherent-state expectation a plain polynomial in $\alpha$ and $\alpha^*$.

source.note: E. C. G. Sudarshan, Physical Review Letters 10 (1963), 277, and R. J. Glauber, Physical Review 131 (1963), 2766.

statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on a smooth manifold $M$. Each orbit of $\mathcal{F}$ (the points joined by finite chains of flows of fields of $\mathcal{F}$) is an immersed submanifold of $M$. Its tangent space at $p$ is spanned by the vectors $(P_*X)(p)$, with $X \in \mathcal{F}$ and $P$ a chain of flows, and it contains the iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket) of $\mathcal{F}$ at $p$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a smooth manifold.
The set $\mathcal{F}$ is any family of smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on $M$, with no condition on rank or brackets.

conclusion: Every orbit is an immersed submanifold, and its tangent space at $p$ is the span of the vectors $(P_*X)(p)$.

proofs.name: Sussmann's invariant distribution
proofs.slogan: Span the pushed-forward fields, show that this distribution is invariant under the flows and has constant rank on an orbit, and build charts from flows.
proofs.scope: Any family, finite or infinite; the orbits partition $M$ into a singular foliation. The proof is an outline of Sussmann's argument, and the analytic case is Nagano's earlier theorem.

roles.why: The fields of $\mathcal{F}$ generate the flows that define the orbits and the distribution.
The smooth manifold structure of $M$ makes the flows diffeomorphisms and gives the charts.

steps.slogan: Define the orbits by finite chains of flows of fields of $\mathcal{F}$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of local diffeomorphisms $e^{t_kX_k}\circ\dots\circ e^{t_1X_1}$ with $X_i \in \mathcal{F}$. The orbit of $q$ is $\{P(q) : P \in \mathcal{P}\}$, and the orbits partition $M$ because $\mathcal{P}$ is closed under composition and inverses.

steps.slogan: Span the pushed-forward fields into a distribution $\Delta$ that every chain of flows preserves.
steps.detail: Let $\Delta(p)$ be the span of the vectors $(P_*X)(p)$ with $X \in \mathcal{F}$ and $P \in \mathcal{P}$. By construction $Q_*\Delta(p) \subseteq \Delta(Q(p))$ for all $Q \in \mathcal{P}$. Differentiating $(e^{-tX})_*Y$ at $t = 0$ gives $[X,Y]$, so $\Delta$ contains the iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket).

steps.slogan: Show that the dimension of $\Delta$ is constant along each orbit.
steps.detail: Each $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ is a diffeomorphism with $Q_*\Delta(p) \subseteq \Delta(Q(p))$, and $Q^{-1} \in \mathcal{P}$ gives the reverse inclusion. So $Q_*$ maps $\Delta(p)$ onto $\Delta(Q(p))$ and $\dim\Delta$ does not change on an orbit.

steps.slogan: Build a local parametrization of the orbit from flows of a basis of $\Delta(p)$.
steps.detail: Choose $Y_i = (P_i)_*X_i$ with $Y_1(p), \dots, Y_m(p)$ a basis of $\Delta(p)$, and set $\Phi(t) = e^{t_1Y_1}\circ\dots\circ e^{t_mY_m}(p)$. Each $e^{tY_i}$ lies in $\mathcal{P}$, so $\Phi$ maps into the orbit, and $d\Phi_0$ is injective. Invariance and constant rank make $\Phi$ an immersion near $0$ with image tangent to $\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Topologize the orbit by these parametrizations and read off its tangent space.
steps.detail: Give the orbit the topology generated by the images $\Phi(U)$ of small open sets. Constant rank shows that these images are the charts of a smooth structure for which the inclusion into $M$ is an immersion with tangent space $\Delta$. So every orbit is an immersed submanifold.

concepts.c:vector-field: The fields of the family and their flows generate the orbits.
concepts.c:lie-bracket: Brackets arise as derivatives of pushed-forward fields, so $\Delta$ contains them.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The manifold structure turns flows into diffeomorphisms and supplies the charts.

source.ref: H. J. Sussmann, Orbits of families of vector fields and integrability of distributions, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 180 (1973), 171-188
source.note: Sussmann proves that the orbits of any set of smooth vector fields are immersed submanifolds with tangent space the span of the pushed-forward fields; Nagano proved the analytic case in J. Math. Soc. Japan 18 (1966), 398-404.

statement: Let $R$ be a ring, $M$ a [Noetherian module](c:noetherian-module) over $R$, and $N$ an $R$-module. If $i, f \colon N \to M$ are [linear maps](c:linear-map) with $i$ injective and $f$ surjective, then $f$ is injective. In particular, a surjection from a [submodule](c:submodule) of $M$ onto $M$ is injective.

hypotheses.text: The module $M$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-module): every ascending chain of submodules is stationary.
The map $i \colon N \to M$ is [injective](c:injective-map).
The map $f \colon N \to M$ is [surjective](c:surjection).

proofs.name: Iterated preimage chain
proofs.slogan: Build the ascending chain $0 \subseteq f^{-1}(i(0)) \subseteq \dots$, stop it by the Noetherian property, and descend the equality back to $\ker f = 0$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for rings that need not be commutative. The case $N = M$ and $i = \mathrm{id}$ gives that a surjective endomorphism of a Noetherian module is injective.

roles.why: The [Noetherian](c:noetherian-module) property of $M$ passes to $N$ and stops the chain.
Injectivity of $i$ embeds $N$ in $M$ and makes the image map on submodules injective.
Surjectivity of $f$ makes the preimage map on submodules injective.

steps.slogan: Build the chain $K_0 = 0$ and $K_{n+1} = f^{-1}(i(K_n))$ of submodules of $N$.
steps.detail: Here $K_1 = f^{-1}(i(0)) = \ker f \supseteq K_0$. The operation $K \mapsto f^{-1}(i(K))$ preserves inclusions, so $K_n \subseteq K_{n+1}$ gives $K_{n+1} \subseteq K_{n+2}$. By induction the $K_n$ form an ascending chain of [submodules](c:submodule).

steps.slogan: Make the chain stationary because $N$ is a Noetherian module.
steps.detail: The injective map $i$ embeds $N$ into the Noetherian module $M$, so $N$ is Noetherian. Hence the [ascending chain](c:ascending-chain-condition) stops: $K_m = K_{m+1}$ for some $m$.

steps.slogan: Descend the equality $K_m = K_{m+1}$ down to $K_0 = K_1$.
steps.detail: If $K_j = K_{j+1}$ with $j \ge 1$, then $f^{-1}(i(K_{j-1})) = f^{-1}(i(K_j))$. Surjectivity of $f$ makes $f^{-1}$ injective on submodules and injectivity of $i$ makes the image map injective, so $K_{j-1} = K_j$. Repeating this $m$ times gives $K_0 = K_1$.

steps.slogan: Read off that the kernel of $f$ is zero.
steps.detail: Since $K_1 = \ker f$ and $K_0 = 0$, the equality $K_0 = K_1$ gives $\ker f = 0$. So $f$ is injective.

concepts.c:noetherian-module: It forces the ascending chain of submodules to stop.
concepts.c:linear-map: The maps $i$ and $f$ are linear, so images and preimages of submodules are submodules.
concepts.c:injective-map: Injectivity of $i$ lets equal images imply equal submodules.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjectivity of $f$ lets equal preimages imply equal submodules.
concepts.c:submodule: The chain consists of submodules of $N$ built by images and preimages.
concepts.c:ascending-chain-condition: Stopping of the chain is the ascending chain condition on $N$.

statement: Let $q$ be a prime power with $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. There is a [Hadamard matrix](c:hadamard-matrix) of order $q+1$, that is, a $\pm 1$ matrix $H$ with $HH^T = (q+1)I$. It is built from the squares of the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$.

hypotheses.text: The number $q$ is a prime power, so the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ exists.
The number $q$ satisfies $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

conclusion: The matrix $H = I + S$ built below is a $\pm 1$ matrix of order $q+1$ with $HH^T = (q+1)I$.

proofs.name: Jacobsthal matrix
proofs.slogan: Build the Jacobsthal matrix from the quadratic character, show $QQ^T = qI - J$ and $Q^T = -Q$, and border it into an orthogonal $\pm 1$ matrix.
proofs.scope: Paley's first construction (type I), for $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. The second construction (type II) gives order $2(q+1)$ for $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

roles.why: The [field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ supplies the quadratic character and the index set of $Q$.
The condition $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ makes $-1$ a nonsquare, so $Q$ is skew.

steps.slogan: Define the Jacobsthal matrix $Q$ from the [quadratic residues](c:quadratic-residue) of $\mathbb{F}_q$.
steps.detail: Let $\chi(x) = 1$ for nonzero squares, $-1$ for nonsquares and $\chi(0) = 0$. The character $\chi$ is multiplicative and $\sum_x \chi(x) = 0$. The matrix $Q_{xy} = \chi(x - y)$ has zero diagonal, entries $\pm 1$ elsewhere, and zero row and column sums, so $Q\mathbf{1} = 0$.

steps.slogan: Compute $QQ^T = qI - J$ from sums of products of characters.
steps.detail: The entry $(x,y)$ of $QQ^T$ is $\sum_u \chi(u)\chi(u+d)$ with $d = y - x$; for $d = 0$ it is $q - 1$. For $d \ne 0$ the terms with $u \ne 0$ equal $\chi(1 + d/u)$, and $1 + d/u$ runs over $\mathbb{F}_q \setminus \{1\}$, so the sum is $0 - \chi(1) = -1$. So $QQ^T = (q-1)I - (J - I) = qI - J$.

steps.slogan: Show that $Q^T = -Q$ because $-1$ is a nonsquare when $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.
steps.detail: The group $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ is cyclic of order $q - 1$ and $-1$ is its element of order 2, so $-1$ is a square exactly when $(q-1)/2$ is even. Here $(q-1)/2$ is odd, so $\chi(-1) = -1$ and $Q_{yx} = \chi(y-x) = -\chi(x-y) = -Q_{xy}$.

steps.slogan: Border $Q$ into a matrix $S$ of order $q+1$ with $SS^T = qI$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \mathbf{1}^T \\ -\mathbf{1} & Q \end{pmatrix}$. Using $Q\mathbf{1} = 0$, $QQ^T = qI - J$ and $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{1} = q$, a block computation gives $SS^T = qI$. By step 3, also $S^T = -S$.

steps.slogan: Set $H = I + S$ and compute $HH^T$.
steps.detail: The matrix $H$ has entries $\pm 1$: its diagonal is $1$ and every off-diagonal entry of $S$ is $\pm 1$. Since $S^T = -S$ and $SS^T = qI$, we get $HH^T = (I + S)(I - S) = I - S^2 = I + SS^T = (q+1)I$.

concepts.c:finite-field: The field carries the quadratic character that defines the matrix $Q$.
concepts.c:quadratic-residue: The squares of the field decide the signs of the entries of $Q$.
concepts.c:hadamard-matrix: The target is a $\pm 1$ matrix whose rows are orthogonal.

source.note: R. E. A. C. Paley, On orthogonal matrices, Journal of Mathematics and Physics 12 (1933), 311-320; the proof is the standard one, as in MacWilliams and Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes (1977).

statement: Let $X$ be a [scheme](c:scheme) and $U \subseteq X$ an open set that is [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact) and [quasi-separated](c:quasi-separated-space). For every $f \in \mathcal{O}_X(U)$, restriction identifies $\mathcal{O}_X(D(f))$ with the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $\mathcal{O}_X(U)_f$, where $D(f) \subseteq U$ is the [basic open set](c:basic-open) of $f$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [scheme](c:scheme), and $f$ is a section of $\mathcal{O}_X$ over the open set $U$.
The open set $U$ is [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact).
The open set $U$ is [quasi-separated](c:quasi-separated-space): two quasi-compact open subsets of $U$ meet in a quasi-compact set.

conclusion: The restriction map makes $\mathcal{O}_X(D(f))$ the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) of $\mathcal{O}_X(U)$ at $f$.

proofs.name: Induction on affine opens
proofs.slogan: Check the three localization axioms: $f$ is a unit on $D(f)$, a power of $f$ kills the kernel, and sections extend after a power of $f$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for $\rho \colon \mathcal{O}(U) \to \mathcal{O}(D(f))$, including the empty $U$, where the ring is zero. The affine case is the base of an induction on the number of affine opens covering $U$.

roles.why: A [scheme](c:scheme) is locally affine, and on affine pieces $D(f)$ is a localization.
[Quasi-compactness](c:quasi-compact) gives a finite affine cover, so one exponent works for all pieces.
[Quasi-separatedness](c:quasi-separated-space) keeps the overlap of two pieces quasi-compact.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ restricts to a unit on $D(f)$.
steps.detail: At each point of the [basic open set](c:basic-open) $D(f)$ the germ of $f$ is a unit of the local ring. A section that is a unit at every stalk is a unit of $\mathcal{O}(D(f))$, by inverting locally and gluing. So $\rho(f)^n$ is a unit for all $n$.

steps.slogan: Settle the case of an [affine scheme](c:affine-scheme), where $D(f) = \operatorname{Spec} A_f$.
steps.detail: If $U = \operatorname{Spec} A$, the basic open set $D(f)$ is $\operatorname{Spec} A_f$, so $\mathcal{O}(D(f)) = A_f$. Then $\rho$ is the localization map $A \to A_f$, and the claim holds.

steps.slogan: Kill a section that vanishes on $D(f)$ by a power of $f$.
steps.detail: Cover $U$ by finitely many affine opens $U_i$, which [quasi-compactness](c:quasi-compact) allows. If $s|_{D(f)} = 0$, the affine case gives $n_i$ with $f^{n_i}s = 0$ on $U_i$. With $N = \max n_i$, the section $f^N s$ vanishes on every $U_i$, hence on $U$.

steps.slogan: Match two local extensions on an overlap after multiplying by a power of $f$.
steps.detail: Write $U = S \cup V$ with $V$ affine and $S$ a union of fewer affine opens, and induct on their number. Take $(n_1, y_1)$ on $S$ and $(n_2, y_2)$ on $V$ with $y_i|_{D(f)} = f^{n_i}t$. On $D(f) \cap S \cap V$ both $f^{n_2}y_1$ and $f^{n_1}y_2$ equal $f^{n_1+n_2}t$, and $S \cap V$ is quasi-compact, so step 3 gives $m$ with $f^{m+n_2}y_1 = f^{m+n_1}y_2$ on $S \cap V$.

steps.slogan: Glue the two extensions into one section on $U$.
steps.detail: The sections $f^{m+n_2}y_1$ on $S$ and $f^{m+n_1}y_2$ on $V$ agree on $S \cap V$, so the sheaf axiom glues them to $y \in \mathcal{O}(U)$. On $D(f) \cap S$ and on $D(f) \cap V$ we have $y = f^{m+n_1+n_2}t$, hence on $D(f)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three facts into the defining properties of the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) at $f$.
steps.detail: Step 1 says that $\rho(f)$ is a unit. Steps 4 and 5 say that every $t \in \mathcal{O}(D(f))$ equals $\rho(y)/\rho(f)^n$. Step 3 says that $\rho(s) = 0$ forces $f^n s = 0$. These three properties characterize $\mathcal{O}(U)_f$.

concepts.c:scheme: A scheme is covered by affine opens, where the claim is algebra.
concepts.c:quasi-compact: It gives finite affine covers, so one exponent serves all pieces.
concepts.c:quasi-separated-space: It keeps the overlaps of affine pieces quasi-compact for the induction.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: The goal is that sections over $D(f)$ form the localization at $f$.
concepts.c:basic-open: The open set $D(f)$ is where $f$ is invertible.
concepts.c:affine-scheme: On an affine scheme the basic open set is the spectrum of a localization.

source.note: mathlib proves the three axioms of IsLocalization.Away: isUnit_res_basicOpen, exists_eq_pow_mul_of_isCompact_of_isQuasiSeparated (compact open induction and gluing) and exists_pow_mul_eq_zero_of_res_basicOpen_eq_zero_of_isCompact; this is Vakil's proof in The Rising Sea.

statement: On the upper half-plane, the [Serre derivative](c:serre-derivative) $\partial_1 E_2 = DE_2 - \tfrac{1}{12}E_2^2$ of the [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) $E_2 = 1 - 24\sum \sigma_1(n)q^n$ equals $-\tfrac{1}{12}E_4$, where $D = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\frac{d}{dz}$.
conclusion: $DE_2 - \tfrac{1}{12}E_2^2 = -\tfrac{1}{12}E_4$ as functions on the upper half-plane.

proofs.name: Weight-four space
proofs.slogan: The defect of $E_2$ cancels in $DE_2 - E_2^2/12$, which is then a level-one form of weight 4 with constant term $-1/12$, so it equals $-E_4/12$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. The space of level-one forms of weight 4 is spanned by $E_4$, so one constant term decides the identity.

steps.slogan: State the transformation law of $E_2$ under $z \mapsto z+1$ and $z \mapsto -1/z$.
steps.detail: $E_2(z+1) = E_2(z)$ and $E_2(-1/z) = z^2E_2(z) + az$ with $a = 12/(2\pi i)$. So $E_2$ is quasi-modular: it has weight 2 up to the defect term $az$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the law of $z \mapsto -1/z$ to get the law of $DE_2$.
steps.detail: Differentiating $E_2(-1/z) = z^2E_2(z) + az$ and multiplying by $z^2/(2\pi i)$ gives $(DE_2)(-1/z) = z^4DE_2(z) + \frac{2}{2\pi i}z^3E_2(z) + \frac{a}{2\pi i}z^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G = DE_2 - E_2^2/12$ satisfies $G(-1/z) = z^4G(z)$.
steps.detail: Squaring the law gives $E_2(-1/z)^2 = z^4E_2^2 + 2az^3E_2 + a^2z^2$. In $G(-1/z)$ the terms $\frac{2}{2\pi i}z^3E_2$ and $\frac{2a}{12}z^3E_2$ cancel because $a = 12/(2\pi i)$. The terms $\frac{a}{2\pi i}z^2$ and $\frac{a^2}{12}z^2$ both equal $\frac{12}{(2\pi i)^2}z^2$ and cancel. Also $G(z+1) = G(z)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $G$ is a [modular form](c:modular-form) of weight 4 for $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
steps.detail: The substitutions $z \mapsto z+1$ and $z \mapsto -1/z$ generate the [modular group](c:modular-group) $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, so $G$ has weight 4 and is holomorphic on the upper half-plane. Its [q-expansion](c:q-expansion) is $G = -\tfrac{1}{12} + O(q)$, so $G$ is holomorphic at the cusp.

steps.slogan: Compare the constant terms of $G$ and $E_4$ in the weight-4 space.
steps.detail: The form $G + \tfrac{1}{12}E_4$ has weight 4 and constant term $-\tfrac{1}{12} + \tfrac{1}{12} = 0$. A level-one form of weight $4 < 12$ with zero constant term vanishes by the Sturm bound. So $G = -\tfrac{1}{12}E_4$.

concepts.c:serre-derivative: The identity computes the Serre derivative, which preserves modularity.
concepts.c:eisenstein-series: The Eisenstein series are the forms whose derivatives are computed.
concepts.c:modular-form: The Serre derivative is a modular form, which a constant term determines.
concepts.c:q-expansion: The $q$-expansion shows holomorphy at the cusp and the constant term.
concepts.c:modular-group: Its two generators reduce the invariance check to two substitutions.

statement: On the upper half-plane, the [Serre derivative](c:serre-derivative) $\partial_4 E_4 = DE_4 - \tfrac{1}{3}E_2E_4$ of the [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) $E_4$ equals $-\tfrac{1}{3}E_6$, where $D = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\frac{d}{dz}$.
conclusion: $DE_4 - \tfrac{1}{3}E_2E_4 = -\tfrac{1}{3}E_6$ as functions on the upper half-plane.

proofs.name: Weight-six space
proofs.slogan: The Serre derivative of $E_4$ is a level-one form of weight 6 with constant term $-1/3$, so it equals $-E_6/3$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. The space of level-one forms of weight 6 is spanned by $E_6$, so one constant term decides the identity.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial_4E_4$ transforms like a form of weight 6.
steps.detail: For $f$ of weight $k$, differentiating $f(\gamma z) = (cz+d)^kf(z)$ adds the term $\frac{kc}{2\pi i}(cz+d)^{k+1}f$ to $(Df)(\gamma z)$. The law $E_2(\gamma z) = (cz+d)^2E_2 + \frac{12c}{2\pi i}(cz+d)$ adds the same term to $\frac{k}{12}E_2f$, so $\partial_kf$ has weight $k+2$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\partial_4E_4$ is holomorphic at the cusp.
steps.detail: In [q-expansions](c:q-expansion), $DE_4 = 240\sum n\sigma_3(n)q^n$ and $E_2E_4$ have no negative powers of $q$. So $\partial_4E_4$ is a [modular form](c:modular-form) of weight 6 for $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

steps.slogan: Compute the constant term of $\partial_4E_4$.
steps.detail: The derivative $D = q\,d/dq$ kills constants, so $DE_4$ has constant term $0$. The product $E_2E_4$ has constant term $1$. So $\partial_4E_4$ has constant term $-\tfrac{4}{12} = -\tfrac{1}{3}$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\partial_4E_4$ with $E_6$ in the weight-6 space.
steps.detail: The form $\partial_4E_4 + \tfrac{1}{3}E_6$ has weight 6 and constant term $0$, so it vanishes by the Sturm bound for level one, since $6 < 12$. Hence $\partial_4E_4 = -\tfrac{1}{3}E_6$.

statement: On the upper half-plane, the [Serre derivative](c:serre-derivative) $\partial_6 E_6 = DE_6 - \tfrac{1}{2}E_2E_6$ of the [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) $E_6$ equals $-\tfrac{1}{2}E_4^2$, where $D = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\frac{d}{dz}$.
conclusion: $DE_6 - \tfrac{1}{2}E_2E_6 = -\tfrac{1}{2}E_4^2$ as functions on the upper half-plane.

proofs.name: Weight-eight space
proofs.slogan: The Serre derivative of $E_6$ is a level-one form of weight 8 with constant term $-1/2$, so it equals $-E_4^2/2$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. The space of level-one forms of weight 8 is spanned by $E_4^2$, so one constant term decides the identity.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial_6E_6$ transforms like a form of weight 8.
steps.detail: For $f$ of weight $k$, differentiating $f(\gamma z) = (cz+d)^kf(z)$ adds the term $\frac{kc}{2\pi i}(cz+d)^{k+1}f$ to $(Df)(\gamma z)$. The law $E_2(\gamma z) = (cz+d)^2E_2 + \frac{12c}{2\pi i}(cz+d)$ adds the same term to $\frac{k}{12}E_2f$, so $\partial_kf$ has weight $k+2$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\partial_6E_6$ is holomorphic at the cusp.
steps.detail: In [q-expansions](c:q-expansion), $DE_6 = -504\sum n\sigma_5(n)q^n$ and $E_2E_6$ have no negative powers of $q$. So $\partial_6E_6$ is a [modular form](c:modular-form) of weight 8 for $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

steps.slogan: Compute the constant term of $\partial_6E_6$.
steps.detail: The derivative $D = q\,d/dq$ kills constants, so $DE_6$ has constant term $0$. The product $E_2E_6$ has constant term $1$. So $\partial_6E_6$ has constant term $-\tfrac{6}{12} = -\tfrac{1}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\partial_6E_6$ with $E_4^2$ in the weight-8 space.
steps.detail: The product $E_4^2$ has weight 8 and constant term $1$. So $\partial_6E_6 + \tfrac{1}{2}E_4^2$ has weight 8 and constant term $0$, and it vanishes by the Sturm bound for level one, since $8 < 12$. Hence $\partial_6E_6 = -\tfrac{1}{2}E_4^2$.

statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space with [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $\mu$, let $s \subseteq E$, and let $f \colon E \to E$ be [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of $s$ with derivative $f'(x)$. If the [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) $\det f'(x)$ is $0$ for all $x \in s$, then $\mu(f(s)) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) within $s$ at each $x \in s$, with derivative $f'(x)$.
The [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) $\det f'(x)$ is $0$ for every $x \in s$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the auxiliary bounded form: for $s$ inside a closed ball of radius $R$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ it gives $\mu(f(s)) \le \varepsilon\,\mu(\bar B(0,R))$. The statement here is the final lemma addHaar_image_eq_zero_of_det_fderivWithin_eq_zero, which lets $\varepsilon \to 0$ and exhausts $s$ by balls.

proofs.name: Nearly linear pieces
proofs.slogan: Split the set into countably many pieces on which $f$ is nearly linear with singular linear part, and bound each image by $\varepsilon$ times the volume.
proofs.scope: No measurability of $s$ is needed, and the case $s = \emptyset$ is trivial. The measure $\mu$ is any Haar measure on $E$.

roles.why: [Differentiability](c:differentiable-function) makes $f$ close to $f'(y)$ on small pieces of $s$.
A zero [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) makes the volume factor $|\det A_n| + \varepsilon$ equal to $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound the volume growth of a map that is close to a linear map $A$.
steps.detail: For linear $A$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that, if $\|f(z) - f(x) - A(z-x)\| \le \delta\|z-x\|$ for $x, z \in t$, then $\mu(f(t)) \le (|\det A| + \varepsilon)\mu(t)$. A ball $\bar B(x,r)$ maps into a $\delta r$-thickening of $f(x) + A(\bar B(0,r))$, whose measure tends to $|\det A|\mu(\bar B(x,r))$. A Besicovitch cover of $t$ by small balls adds these bounds.

steps.slogan: Cover $s$ by countably many measurable pieces on which $f$ is close to some $f'(y_n)$.
steps.detail: Differentiability at each $x \in s$ gives a neighborhood where $f$ is within $\delta/2$ of $f'(x)$ in the sense of step 1. Countable dense sets in $E$ and in the space of operators give disjoint measurable sets $t_n$ covering $s$ and points $y_n \in s$ such that $f$ is $\delta(A_n)$-close to $A_n = f'(y_n)$ on $s \cap t_n$.

steps.slogan: Add the volume bounds over the pieces of $s$ inside a ball.
steps.detail: Let $s \subseteq \bar B(0,R)$. By subadditivity and step 1, $\mu(f(s)) \le \sum_n (|\det A_n| + \varepsilon)\mu(s \cap t_n)$. Here $\det A_n = \det f'(y_n) = 0$, so the sum is at most $\varepsilon \sum_n \mu(\bar B(0,R) \cap t_n) \le \varepsilon\,\mu(\bar B(0,R))$, as the $t_n$ are disjoint.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero to get measure zero for bounded pieces.
steps.detail: The bound $\mu(f(s)) \le \varepsilon\,\mu(\bar B(0,R))$ holds for every $\varepsilon > 0$, and $\mu(\bar B(0,R))$ is finite. So $\mu(f(s)) = 0$ whenever $s \subseteq \bar B(0,R)$.

steps.slogan: Write $s$ as a countable union of bounded pieces.
steps.detail: Apply step 4 to $s \cap \bar B(0,k)$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Countable subadditivity gives $\mu(f(s)) \le \sum_k \mu(f(s \cap \bar B(0,k))) = 0$.

concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The image is shown to be null for this measure, with volume scaling by determinants.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives the linear approximations on small pieces.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: Its vanishing makes the volume factor of each linear piece zero.

source.note: mathlib uses addHaar_image_le_mul_of_det_lt (volume growth near a linear map, with the Besicovitch covering) and exists_partition_approximatesLinearOn_of_hasFDerivWithinAt; the final lemma lets epsilon tend to 0 and exhausts by balls.

statement: Let $a \le b$, let $f \colon [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be nonincreasing ([monotone](c:monotone-function)) with $f(b) \ge 0$, and let $g$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a,b]$. Then $\int_a^b fg = f(a)\int_a^\xi g$ for some $\xi \in [a,b]$.

hypotheses.text: The endpoints satisfy $a \le b$.
The function $f$ is nonincreasing ([monotone](c:monotone-function)) on $[a,b]$.
The value $f(b)$ is nonnegative.
The function $g$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a,b]$.

proofs.name: Layer cake and primitive
proofs.slogan: Write $f$ as an integral of level sets, swap the integrals, bound each level integral between the extremes of the primitive of $g$, and use the intermediate value theorem.
proofs.scope: The nonincreasing form of Bonnet's theorem; the nondecreasing form and Weierstrass' two-term form are the other members of the family. The case $f(a) = 0$ is treated separately.

roles.why: The interval $[a,b]$ is compact and nonempty, so the primitive of $g$ has extreme points.
A [monotone](c:monotone-function) $f$ gives measurable level sets that are intervals starting at $a$.
The inequality $f(b) \ge 0$ gives $0 \le f(x) \le f(a)$, which the layer formula needs.
[Integrability](c:integrable-function) of $g$ allows Fubini and makes its primitive continuous.

steps.slogan: Write $f(x)$ as the integral of an indicator over the height $r$.
steps.detail: For $x \in [a,b]$ we have $0 \le f(b) \le f(x) \le f(a)$, so $f(x) = \int_0^{f(a)} \mathbf{1}_{\{r \le f(x)\}}\,dr$. Hence $f(x)g(x) = \int_0^{f(a)} \mathbf{1}_{\{r \le f(x)\}}\,g(x)\,dr$.

steps.slogan: Swap the order of integration with Fubini's theorem.
steps.detail: The region $\{(x,r) : r \le f(x)\}$ is measurable because $f$ is monotone, and $g(x)\mathbf{1}$ is integrable on $[a,b] \times [0,f(a)]$. Fubini gives $\int_a^b fg = \int_0^{f(a)} H(r)\,dr$ with $H(r) = \int_a^b \mathbf{1}_{\{r \le f(x)\}}g(x)\,dx$.

steps.slogan: Show that each $H(r)$ equals $G(c_r)$, where $G(x) = \int_a^x g$.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is nonincreasing, the set $\{x \in [a,b] : r \le f(x)\}$ is an interval that starts at $a$ and ends at some $c_r$, with or without its endpoint. A single point has measure zero, so $H(r) = \int_a^{c_r} g = G(c_r)$ for $0 \le r \le f(a)$.

steps.slogan: Bound $H(r)$ between the minimum and the maximum of the [primitive](c:antiderivative) $G$.
steps.detail: The primitive $G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ because $g$ is integrable. By the extreme value theorem it has a minimum at $\xi_1$ and a maximum at $\xi_2$, so $G(\xi_1) \le H(r) \le G(\xi_2)$ for $r \in [0,f(a)]$. Integrating over $r$ gives $f(a)G(\xi_1) \le \int_a^b fg \le f(a)G(\xi_2)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $f(a)$ and apply the intermediate value theorem to $G$.
steps.detail: If $f(a) = 0$, then $0 \le f \le f(a)$ gives $f = 0$ on $[a,b]$, and $\xi = a$ works. If $f(a) > 0$, the number $\int_a^b fg / f(a)$ lies between $G(\xi_1)$ and $G(\xi_2)$, so the intermediate value theorem gives $\xi \in [a,b]$ with $G(\xi) = \int_a^b fg / f(a)$.

concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity makes the level sets of $f$ intervals that start at $a$.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $g$ allows Fubini and gives a continuous primitive.
concepts.c:antiderivative: The primitive $G$ has extreme values that bracket every level integral.

source.note: mathlib writes f as a layer-cake integral and swaps with intervalIntegral_intervalIntegral_swap, shows that each level integral lies in the range of the primitive G (extreme values on isCompact_Icc), and finishes with IsPreconnected.intermediate_value.
